problems.title: Polygonal chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 1. Polygonal chemistry

The palladium complex $\ce{[Pd(NO3)2(TMEDA)]}$ reacts with sodium isonicotinate (simplified as NaL) in a 1 : 1 ratio to yield a mixture of multinuclear complexes $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$, which resemble the simplest equilateral polygons by structure. The empirical formula of both complexes is $\ce{[PdL(TMEDA)]NO3}$, where $\mathbf{A}$ can exist as four different isomers ($\mathbf{A^1}$–$\mathbf{A^4}$) and $\mathbf{B}$ as two isomers ($\mathbf{B^1}$–$\mathbf{B^2}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-1-fig1.png

a) Write the systematic name for the complex $\ce{[Pd(NO3)2(TMEDA)]}$.

b) Sketch the structures of inner coordination spheres of complexes $\mathbf{A^1}$–$\mathbf{A^4}$ and $\mathbf{B^1}$–$\mathbf{B^2}$ using the provided structural simplifications to represent TMEDA and the isonicotinate anion ($\ce{L^-}$). Ignore overall charges and counterions in your structures.

Complexes $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ can interconvert in solution. Their chemical equilibrium is described by the equation $a\mathbf{A} \rightleftharpoons b\mathbf{B}$, where $a$ and $b$ are integer coefficients. The forward equilibrium constant has a value $K_1 = 21.5$ at $t_1 = 40.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $K_2 = 32.1$ at $t_2 = 60.0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. For the sake of simplicity, assume all isomers of $\mathbf{A}$ have the same Gibbs free energy of formation and all isomers of $\mathbf{B}$ also have the same Gibbs free energy of formation.

c) Determine the smallest possible integer values for coefficients $a$ and $b$.

d) Calculate the value of the forward equilibrium constant $K_3$ at $t_3 = 50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

e) Approximate the ratio $[\mathbf{B}] : [\mathbf{A}]$ in solution at $t_3 = 50\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ if the analytical concentration of palladium in solution is $c_0 = 1.154\,\mathrm{mM}$. Assume that in solution, $\ce{Pd^{2+}}$ exists only as part of complexes $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$.

problems.title: Unknown amino acid
problems.problem:
Problem 2. Unknown amino acid

$0.3425\,\mathrm{g}$ of unknown amino acid $\mathbf{X}$ sample was treated with hot concentrated sulphuric acid, which converts organically bound nitrogen to ammonium salt. Then, an excess of concentrated sodium hydroxide solution was added to the previously obtained solution containing ammonium ions. Generated ammonia was distilled into $40.00\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1350 M hydrochloric acid. Finally, the excess of hydrochloric acid was titrated with $16.83\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1500 M sodium hydroxide solution. In the following calculations, assume that all produced ammonia reacts with hydrochloric acid.

a) Calculate the mass percentage (%) of nitrogen in the sample.

b) Calculate the pH value of the hydrochloric acid solution after the titration when $16.83\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of 0.1500 M sodium hydroxide solution has been added. $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a}(\ce{NH4^+}) = 9.25$.

In nature, $\mathbf{X}$ occurs in its $L$-isomer form, which has two adjacent stereocenters. The dissociation constants of $\mathbf{X}$ are $K_\mathrm{a1} = 8.13\cdot10^{-3}$ and $K_\mathrm{a2} = 7.94\cdot10^{-10}$ ($25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$).

c) Determine the condensed structural formula of $\mathbf{X}$.

d) Draw all the possible stereochemical structures for $\mathbf{X}$ using wedge-dash notation. Indicate the absolute configurations ($R$/$S$) of the stereocenters on all the structures.

e) Select from the table above and draw the stereochemical structures of $\mathbf{X}$ $L$-isomer for the major ionic forms in aqueous solution at (i) pH 1.50, (ii) pH 6.00, and (iii) pH 11.00.

f) Calculate the pH value of the aqueous $\mathbf{X}$ solution at its isoelectric point, where the overall charge of the ionic amino acid species is zero.

problems.title: Reverse engineering
problems.problem:
Problem 3. Reverse engineering

A teacher is making a standard kinetics task for an exam, starting from desired answers that are easy to grade – 30 s and $60\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Assist him in making the task! Consider a first-order kinetic reaction $\mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{B}$ at $T_1 = 300\,\mathrm{K}$. The initial concentration $[\mathrm{A}]_0$ is 1 M, and the concentration $[\mathrm{A}]_t$ after time $t$ is 0.05 M.

a) Calculate the reaction rate constant $k$ value corresponding to $t = 30\,\mathrm{s}$.

b) Calculate the activation energy $E_\mathrm{a}$ value corresponding to $t = 3\,\mathrm{s}$ at $T_2 = 2024\,\mathrm{K}$.

The calculated $E_\mathrm{a}$ value turns out to be too small. Which parameters (if changed individually) can the teacher adjust to make up a more reasonable activation energy?

c) Select parameter(s) that affect activation energy $E_\mathrm{a}$: $T_1$, $[\mathrm{A}]_0$, $[\mathrm{A}]_t$, $t$.

d) Recalculate the values of the selected parameters to give $E_\mathrm{a} = 60\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$.

The teacher continued reverse engineering by designing a four-step mechanism that gives a desired reaction law ($-\mathrm{d}[\mathrm{A}]/\mathrm{d}t = 2k_1k_2[\mathrm{A}]/(k_{-1}+2k_2)$) assuming a steady state for A′ and B′:

$$\begin{array}{llcll} \mathrm{A} \rightarrow \mathrm{A'} + \mathrm{B} & (k_1) & \qquad & \ldots + \ldots \rightarrow \ldots + \ldots + \mathrm{C} & (k_2) \\ \ldots + \ldots \rightarrow \mathrm{A} & (k_{-1}) & \qquad & \mathrm{A'} + \mathrm{B'} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B} & (k_3) \end{array}$$

e) Write the equations for the missing elementary steps. Show that your mechanism corresponds to the given reaction law.

problems.title: Have you heard about cerium?
problems.problem:
Problem 4. Have you heard about cerium?

Part I. Minerals

Monazite $\ce{(Ce,La,Nd,Th)PO4}$ and Bastnäsite $\ce{(Ce,La)CO3F}$ are the most common natural sources for cerium and other lanthanides such as lanthanum or neodymium. The monazite structure is made up of the arrangement of separate $\ce{PO4}$ tetrahedra, which are somewhat distorted but joined to one another by Ce (or other lanthanide) atoms. Monazite has a primitive monoclinic lattice system with $\alpha = \gamma = 90^\circ$ and $\beta = 103.63^\circ$. The structure of this mineral is shown (colors of atoms: Ce – grey, P – blue, O – red).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-4-fig1.png

a) How many atoms are in the unit cell of monazite-(Ce)? Hint: A unit cell is the smallest group of atoms from which the entire lattice can be built up by repetition in three dimensions.

b) Presence of which element makes the natural monazite radioactive: i) La, ii) Nd, iii) Th?

Part of the Ce atoms were artificially substituted by U atoms in the pure $\ce{CePO4}$ monazite crystal of 15.23 g. The mass of the resulting mineral was 19.76 g.

c) Calculate the fraction of Ce atoms that were replaced.

U–Pb dating is one of the oldest and most refined of the radiometric dating schemes. The method relies on two separate decay chains, the uranium series from $\ce{^{238}U}$ to $\ce{^{206}Pb}$, with a half-life of 4.47 billion years, and the actinium series from $\ce{^{235}U}$ to $\ce{^{207}Pb}$, with a half-life of 710 million years. Since the exact rate at which uranium decays into lead is known, the current ratio of lead to uranium in a sample of the mineral can be used to reliably determine its age if any lead found in the mineral is radiogenic. Consider a monazite rock (from Kollam, India) of 6.05 g which has 0.37% $\ce{^{238}U2O3}$ and 0.01% PbO by mass.

d) Calculate the approximate age of this mineral. Assume that only the uranium series decay chain occurs, and the presence of Pb is only due to the decay of radioactive $\ce{^{238}U}$.

Bastnäsite usually occurs in a reddish brown color and can even be yellow depending on the ratio of metal ions present in the mineral. To identify the empirical formula of bastnäsite, the specimen with the formula of $\mathrm{Ce_{0.48}La_{\mathit{x}}Nd_{\mathit{y}}Pr_{0.04}Sm_{0.01}CO_3F}$ and weighing 3.1184 g was taken from Gallinas Mountains in New Mexico, USA. During mineral analysis, 0.6260 g of $\ce{CO2}$ after acidic treatment with diluted $\ce{H2SO4}$ was captured.

e) Find an empirical formula for this mineral sample if all metal atoms have an oxidation number +3.

The crystal structure of bastnäsite is quite complex. Yet, one can simplify it to hexagonal closest-packed (HCP) unit cell. In the Figure, Ce atoms are orange, and all other atoms (whether they are C, O, or F) are black.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-4-fig2.png

f) What is the coordination number of Ce in this structure?

Among lanthanides, cerium is the easiest to extract from its minerals because it is the only one that can reach a stable +4 oxidation number in aqueous solutions. While roasting the bastnäsite, most of the lanthanides are oxidized to $\ce{Ln2O3}$, except cerium which forms the water-insoluble dioxide $\ce{CeO2}$.

g) Calculate the volume $\mathrm{m^3}$ of 0.50 M HCl needed to leach $\ce{CeO2}$ after roasting $5.00\cdot10^{3}\,\mathrm{kg}$ of bastnäsite with 32% Ce by mass. Write the equation of this extraction reaction in the tank.

Four allotropic forms of cerium exist at standard pressure. The stable form below $726\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to approximately room temperature is γ-cerium, with a face-centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure. The double hexagonal close-packed form (DHCP), known as β-cerium, is the equilibrium structure approximately from room temperature to $-150\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Upon cooling below $-15\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, γ-cerium starts to change to β-cerium, but the transformation proceeds slowly.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-4-fig3.png

h) Calculate and compare the density of β-cerium ($a = 0.3681\,\mathrm{nm}$, $c = 1.1857\,\mathrm{nm}$) and γ-cerium ($a = 0.5161\,\mathrm{nm}$) in $\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$.

Part II. Cerium loves redox

Cerium extracted from the ores is used to produce certain laboratory reagents such as ceric ammonium nitrate (abbreviated as CAN) $\ce{(NH4)2[Ce(NO3)6]}$. CAN is often used in redox reactions for quantitative analysis, especially iron determination. Consider the reaction of CAN with the soil sample.

i) Write the ionic equation of this one-electron oxidizing reagent reacting with the mixture of green rust $\ce{Fe(OH)2}$ and 4 times smaller amounts of cuprite $\ce{Cu2O}$ in acidic conditions.

j) Draw the structure of the anion of CAN if the central atom and its neighbors form an icosahedron.

$\mathbf{A}$ is a pale white powder and contains 25.11% O by mass. By modifying the oxidation number of oxygen atoms in $\mathbf{A}$, a reddish-brown color substance $\mathbf{B}$ is formed. $\mathbf{B}$ contains oxygens that differ in their oxidation numbers. $\mathbf{B}$ is converted to $\mathbf{C}$ by heating the solution and can be prepared using strong oxidizers like $\ce{PbO2}$. All oxygen atoms in $\mathbf{C}$ have the same oxidation number.

k) Identify $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{C}$ and write the equations: i) $\ce{Ce + H2O} \rightarrow \mathbf{A} + \ce{H2}$, ii) $\mathbf{A} + \ce{HO2^-} \rightarrow \mathbf{B} + \ce{H2O + OH^-}$, iii) $\mathbf{B} + \ce{H2O + OH^-} \rightarrow \mathbf{C} + \ce{HO2^-}$.

l) Fill in the gaps in the text and choose correct answers.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-4-fig4.png

Ceria ($\ce{CeO2}$) plays a special role in heterogeneous catalysis. In the ideal lattice of $\ce{CeO2}$, the structure consists of a primitive cubic / body-centered cubic / face-centered cubic unit cells of cations with anions occupying the cubical / tetrahedral / octahedral holes. In the structure, each cerium cation is coordinated by ____ nearest-neighbor oxygen anions, while each oxygen anion is coordinated by ____ nearest-neighbor cerium cations. Ceria can also be doped with other metal cations to alter electric conductivity. When cerium cations are replaced with lower oxidation number elements ($\ce{M^{2+}}$/$\ce{M^{3+}}$), the lattice oxygen atoms in $\ce{CeO2}$ are incorporated / removed. The ceria crystal usually exhibits a few defects due to the co-existence of $\ce{Ce^{4+}}$ and ________ ions.

One of the applications of $\ce{CeO2}$ resides in automotive catalysis and offers a more efficient way to convert CO to $\ce{CO2}$. The challenging part here is that the oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons must be carried out simultaneously with the reduction of pollutant $\mathbf{I}$. The harsh conditions experienced in the catalytic converter dictate that the catalysts be based on precious metals (e.g., Pt, Rh, and Pd), but precious metals are not selective for oxidizing CO and hydrocarbons using $\mathbf{I}$ in the presence of $\mathbf{J}$. However, an altered catalyst is made by vapor depositing catalytic metals onto polycrystalline ceria films to improve the situation. When excess $\mathbf{J}$ is present in the exhaust stream, it is removed by adsorption onto reduced ceria so that CO and hydrocarbons are oxidized by reducing $\mathbf{J}$. When there are insufficient amounts of $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$ in the exhaust to oxidize the CO and hydrocarbons, ceria releases $\mathbf{K}$. $\mathbf{K}$ transfer from ceria to precious metal is important for catalysis. In excess CO, the kinetics for this reaction over bulk Pt, Pd, and Rh are very well understood and are described by Reactions 1-4 (written in the end), where $\sigma$ represents an empty site on the metal. Because the metal surfaces are essentially saturated in CO when excess CO is present, the rate-limiting step for the reaction is ___. With ceria-supported metals, there is an additional pathway $\mathbf{5}$ for forming $\mathrm{O_{ad}}$ by the transfer of oxygen from ceria to the metal that speeds up the overall conversion. Because ceria does not adsorb CO, the reoxidation of $\mathbf{L}$, reaction $\mathbf{6}$, is not affected by the coverage of CO on the metal. Using steam as the oxidant, $\mathbf{6}$ is replaced by $\mathbf{7}$ which is a very important reaction for the production of $\mathbf{M}$.

$$\begin{array}{l} \text{1) } \mathrm{CO} + \sigma \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_{ad}} \\ \text{2) } \mathrm{O_2} + \sigma \rightarrow \mathrm{O_{2,ad}} \\ \text{3) } \mathrm{O_{2,ad}} + \sigma \rightarrow 2\mathrm{O_{ad}} \\ \text{4) } \mathrm{CO_{ad}} + \mathrm{O_{ad}} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\sigma \end{array}$$

m) Identify formulas of compounds and elements $\mathbf{I}$, $\mathbf{J}$, $\mathbf{K}$, $\mathbf{L}$, and $\mathbf{M}$.

n) Write equations of reactions $\mathbf{5}$, $\mathbf{6}$, and $\mathbf{7}$.

Ce (IV) forms 8-coordinate bis(salen) complexes. A 5,5′-$\ce{X2}$-salen ligand is shown.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-4-fig5.png

o) Which complex – $\mathrm{Ce(5,5'\text{-}(OMe)_2\text{-}salen)_2}$ or $\mathrm{Ce(5,5'\text{-}(Cl)_2\text{-}salen)_2}$ – is a stronger oxidizing agent?

problems.title: Poisonous chemicals
problems.problem:
Problem 5. Poisonous chemicals

$S$-[2-(diisopropylamino)ethyl]-$O$-ethyl methylphosphonothioate ($\mathbf{VX}$) is an odorless, colorless, human-made chemical developed in 1952. It is the most toxic, rapidly acting of all compounds classified as nerve agents. Not found naturally in the environment, $\mathbf{VX}$'s only application is in chemical warfare. It is classified as a weapon of mass destruction by the United Nations in UN Resolution 687, and the production and stockpiling of $\mathbf{VX}$ was outlawed by the Chemical Weapons Convention of 1993. The synthesis of VXs starts with a two-step reaction of phosphorus trichloride with methyl iodide.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-5-fig1.png

a) Draw the structural formula of intermediate $\mathbf{A}$.

b) Draw the structural formulas of compounds $\mathbf{B}$–$\mathbf{D}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-5-fig2.png

Affected by high temperature product $\mathbf{D}$ starts isomerisation to $\mathbf{VX}$.

c) Draw the isomerization mechanism from product $\mathbf{D}$ to $\mathbf{VX}$.

$\mathbf{VX}$ is produced via the thermal process, which gives a racemic mixture of enantiomers.

d) Mark chiral centers in $\mathbf{VX}$ molecule.

e) How many possible stereoisomers does $\mathbf{VX}$ have?

Like other organophosphorus nerve agents, $\mathbf{VX}$ may be destroyed by a reaction with strong nucleophiles. The reaction of $\mathbf{VX}$ with concentrated aqueous sodium hydroxide results in two competing solvolysis reactions, giving four different compounds ($\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{H}$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-5-fig3.png

f) Write structural formulas of compounds $\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{H}$.

g) Which one of the $\mathbf{E}$–$\mathbf{H}$ compounds is still highly toxic?

Despite solvolysis, it was found that $\mathbf{VX}$ can go the third way of degradation. The third degradation pathway becomes dominant under certain conditions. It involves the C–S bond cleavage to form products $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-5-fig4.png

h) Draw the structural formulas of compounds $\mathbf{I}$ and $\mathbf{J}$.

The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum of the $\mathbf{VX}$ (in $\ce{CDCl3}$) is given below.

i) Assign the corresponding $\ce{^1H}$ NMR signals for $\mathbf{VX}$.

j) Indicate chemical element(s) that cause peak splitting in compound $\mathbf{VX}$ $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum.

k) Assign the multiplicity of peaks ($\mathbf{1}$–$\mathbf{6}$) in the $\ce{^1H}$ NMR spectrum.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-5-fig5.png

The agent A-234 is supposedly around five to eight times more potent than $\mathbf{VX}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-5-fig6.png

The median inhaled A-234 lethal dose for an 80 kg person has been estimated as $7\,\mathrm{mg\,m^{-3}}$ for two-minute exposure when the person inhales $15\,\mathrm{dm^3}$ per minute.

l) Calculate the lethal dose of agent A-234 in grams.

m) Calculate the lethal dose in grams per kilogram of a person’s weight.

n) How many lethal doses are in 1 gram of this compound for a 100 kg person?

problems.title: Simple organic chemistry
problems.problem:
Problem 6. Simple organic chemistry

Alkenes react with halogens through a three-membered cationic halonium ion intermediate $\mathbf{Hal^+}$, which is in resonance with a carbocation $\mathbf{Carb^+}$. Both resonance forms explain selectivity in this reaction: halonium $\mathbf{Hal^+}$ dictates that the addition of $\ce{X2}$ is anti (on opposite sides), and carbocation $\mathbf{Carb^+}$ dictates that attack of halide anion (or a different nucleophile) takes place at the most substituted carbon atom.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-6-fig1.png

Let us look at monoalkenes with a molecular formula of $\ce{C5H8}$. Assume that all these isomers are stable and obtainable.

a) Determine the number of i) 5-membered ring, ii) 4-membered ring, and iii) 3-membered ring isomers, considering stereochemistry.

A symmetrical isomer of this group reacted with $\ce{Br2}$ in a nonpolar solvent and formed only one stereoisomer.

b) Draw the structural formula of this isomer.

c) What would be the product of bromination in methanol?

A monoalkene $\mathbf{H1}$ with a molecular formula $\ce{C4H6}$ reacted with bromine and produced three structural isomers $\mathbf{B1}$–$\mathbf{B3}$. The $\ce{^1H}$ NMR data of $\mathbf{B1}$–$\mathbf{B3}$ (in $\ce{CDCl3}$) are given below.

• $\mathbf{B1}$: $\ce{^1H}$ NMR 4.02 (s, 2H), 1.38–1.32 (m, 2H), 1.10–1.03 (m, 2H)
• $\mathbf{B2}$: $\ce{^1H}$ NMR 5.67 (s, 2H), 4.31 (s, 4H)
• $\mathbf{B3}$: $\ce{^1H}$ NMR 3.24 (m, 4H), 2.20 (m, 2H)

d) Draw the structural formulas of compounds $\mathbf{H1}$ and $\mathbf{B1}$–$\mathbf{B3}$.

The formation of halonium ion is typically used as an intermediate in more complex transformations. For example, the Prevost reaction allows to obtain diesters in an anti-fashion:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-6-fig2.png

e) How many stereoisomers are formed in this reaction if i) $(\mathrm{R1} = \mathrm{R2}) \neq \mathrm{H}$ and ii) $(\mathrm{R1} \neq \mathrm{R2}) \neq \mathrm{H}$? Since the product (diester) has 2 chiral carbon atoms, how many stereoisomers exist in total if i) $(\mathrm{R1} = \mathrm{R2}) \neq \mathrm{H}$ and ii) $(\mathrm{R1} \neq \mathrm{R2}) \neq \mathrm{H}$?

f) Draw the mechanism of the Prevost reaction. Note that the relative configuration of the product is anti.

Halonium ion can also be used as an intermediate in the synthesis of 1,2-diamines:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-6-fig3.png

g) Draw the structural formulas of compounds $\mathbf{A1}$–$\mathbf{A3}$, including stereochemistry.

Halonium ion is also an intermediate in some rearrangements, such as semipinacol rearrangement, which leads to a ring expansion:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2024-6-fig4.png

h) Draw the reaction mechanism.

Problem 1. Thermodynamics of fuel cells (10 points)

The following data might be helpful in the task. Assume that the given quantities are independent of temperature.

$$\begin{array}{l|c|c|c|c} & \Delta_f H^\circ\ [\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}] & S^\circ\ [\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}\,K^{-1}}] & \mathrm{MW}\ [\mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}] & \rho\ [\mathrm{g\,L^{-1}}] \\ \hline \ce{HCOOH(l)} & -425.51 & 131.84 & 46.03 & 1220 \\ \hline \ce{H2O(l)} & -285.83 & 69.95 & 18.02 & - \\ \hline \ce{CO2(g)} & -393.52 & 213.79 & 44.01 & - \\ \hline \ce{O2(g)} & - & 205.15 & 32.00 & - \\ \hline \ce{H2(g)} & - & 130.68 & 2.02 & 0.090 \end{array}$$

The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell is:

$$\ce{H2(g) + 1/2 O2(g) -> H2O(l)} \qquad \Delta_r G^\circ = -226.08\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$$

a) Calculate the standard potential ($E^\circ$) for the reaction at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

The thermal energy efficiency of the fuel cell is defined as the amount of useful electrochemical energy produced ($|\Delta G|$) relative to the change in stored chemical energy ($|\Delta H|$).

b) Calculate the efficiency of an ideal hydrogen fuel cell.

A real hydrogen fuel cell operates at a potential ($E$) of $0.80\,\mathrm{V}$.

c) Calculate the energy efficiency for the real hydrogen fuel cell.

Besides efficiency, to determine the applicability of fuel cells, useful quantities are the gravimetric energy density ($\Delta G/m$) and volumetric energy density ($\Delta G/V$), describing the total electrochemical energy released per mass or volume of the reactant, respectively. The commonly used units for these quantities are $\mathrm{kWh\,kg^{-1}}$ for the gravimetric energy density, and $\mathrm{kWh\,L^{-1}}$ for the volumetric energy density.

d) Calculate the gravimetric energy density expressed in $\mathrm{kWh\,kg^{-1}}$ for hydrogen at $298\,\mathrm{K}$. $1\,\mathrm{W} = 1\,\mathrm{J\,s^{-1}}$.

e) Calculate the volumetric energy density expressed in $\mathrm{kWh\,L^{-1}}$ for hydrogen at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

To achieve higher volumetric energy density, the hydrogen can be pressurised. A typical pressurized $\ce{H2}$ cylinder has a pressure of $700\,\mathrm{bar}$.

f) Calculate the volumetric energy density for the pressurised hydrogen. Assume that hydrogen behaves as an ideal gas.

One of the alternatives to the hydrogen fuel cell is a formic acid fuel cell, with the overall reaction:

$$\ce{HCOOH(l) + 1/2 O2(g) -> CO2(g) + H2O(l)}$$

g) Calculate the standard Gibbs free energy ($\Delta_r G^\circ$) and the standard potential ($E^\circ$) for the reaction at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

h) Calculate the gravimetric energy density expressed in $\mathrm{kWh\,kg^{-1}}$ for formic acid at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

i) Calculate the volumetric energy density expressed in $\mathrm{kWh\,L^{-1}}$ for formic acid at $298\,\mathrm{K}$.

problems.title: From tryptophan to melatonin
problems.problem:
Problem 2. From tryptophan to melatonin (10 points)

$L$-tryptophan (Trp) is an essential amino acid. It plays a crucial role in the production of niacin (vitamin $\mathrm{B_3}$), the synthesis of the neurotransmitter serotonin, as well as the hormone melatonin. The acid dissociation constant values of Trp: $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a1} = 2.38$ and $\mathrm{p}K_\mathrm{a2} = 9.39$ at $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-2-fig1.png

a) Calculate the following molar fractions of $L$-tryptophan at its isoelectric point, where the overall charge of the molecule is zero:

i) $\alpha_\mathrm{carboxyl}$ of the ionogenic carboxyl group;

ii) $\alpha_\mathrm{amino}$ of the ionogenic amino group;

iii) $\alpha_\mathrm{neutral}$ of the completely neutral (uncharged) form of Trp.

b) A $1.00\,\mathrm{g}$ sample of Trp is dissolved in $50.0\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ of deionized water. Calculate the equilibrium concentrations ($\mathrm{mol\cdot dm^{-3}}$) of all forms of $L$-tryptophan $[\mathrm{Trp^+}]$, $[\mathrm{Trp^0}]$, and $[\mathrm{Trp^-}]$ present in the solution.

The concentration of Trp can be determined spectrophotometrically. In the chromogenic Hopkins-Cole reaction, a crimson-coloured, light-absorbing product is formed when Trp reacts with glyoxylic acid in a $2 : 1$ molar ratio in the presence of an oxidizing agent. The left graph shows the linear correlation between different Trp concentrations and absorbance at $525\,\mathrm{nm}$. The right graph illustrates the change in absorbance at $525\,\mathrm{nm}$ of a $50\,\mathrm{mg\cdot dm^{-3}}$ Trp solution at different pH levels. The measurements were taken using a cuvette with an optical path length of exactly $1\,\mathrm{cm}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-2-fig2.png

c) Calculate:

i) the concentration ($\mathrm{g\cdot dm^{-3}}$) of a Trp solution, given that its measured absorbance is $0.785$.

ii) the theoretical molar absorption coefficient $\varepsilon$ ($\mathrm{dm^3\cdot mol^{-1}\cdot cm^{-1}}$) of the crimson-coloured Trp solution at pH 5.

Melatonin, produced by the pineal gland, plays a key role in regulating the sleep-wake cycle. The possible EI (electron ionization) fragmentation pathways of the melatonin’s molecular ion $[\mathbf{M}]^+$ are shown in the following scheme:

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-2-fig3.png

The corresponding mass spectrum of melatonin with some additional fragment peaks is given below. Note that the mass spectrum does not display all possible fragment peaks.

Problem 3. Spinel structures (10 points)

Spinels are naturally occuring crystals. Most commonly they exist as binary metal oxides ($\ce{AB2O4}$). The crystal structure of normal spinels is characterized by a cubic lattice comprising 8 cubic subunits $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ in which oxygen atoms form a face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice. In $\mathbf{b}$ structure A metal ion occupies two tetrahedral voids, while in both subunits B ion occupies octahedral voids. Some compounds adopt an inverse spinel structure in which half of ions in octahedral voids occupy tetrahedral voids and all tetrahedrally coordinated ions occupy octahedral voids.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-3-fig1.png

a) How many $\ce{AB2O4}$ formula units are in the spinel unit cell?

b) What percentage of tetrahedral and octahedral voids A and B ions occupy in normal structure?

c) What percentage of tetrahedral and octahedral voids are occupied by A and B in inverse spinel structure?

d) Express smallest A–O distance in normal spinel in terms of unit cell length $l$. Assume that the structure is ideal.

$\ce{MgAl2O4}$ is a prototype compound of the spinel structural family. It can form solid solutions with an excess of $\ce{MgO}$. When $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ cations, which have a lower valency, substitute $\ce{Al^{3+}}$ cations, two main mechanisms help maintain electrical balance. The first mechanism involves addition of cations to interstitial sites, while the second involves the creation of oxygen vacancies.

e) At what ratio $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ ions substitute $\ce{Al^{3+}}$ ions, when charge balance is preserved by adding cations to interstitial sites?

f) How many oxygen ion vacancies per substitutional $\ce{Mg^{2+}}$ are needed to preserve electroneutrality? Hint: the ratio is not necessarily a whole number

Assume that reaction goes to full completion and charge balance is maintained by adding forming cations to interstitials sites.

In spinel structures a metal ion preference for tetrahedral or octahedral sites can be determined by Crystal Field Theory (CFT). The coordination environment that provides greater crystal field stabilization energy (CSFE) is preferred for the metal ion to occupy. Crystal field stabilization energy can be expressed in terms of the crystal field splitting energy ($\Delta$). The crystal field splitting energy in octahedral and tetrahedral environments can be compared by using this equation:

$$\Delta_t \approx \tfrac{4}{9}\Delta_o$$

where $\Delta_t$ and $\Delta_o$ are crystal field splitting energy in tetrahedral and octahedral coordination environments, respectively.

problems.problem:
Problem 5. From diatomics to solids (10 points)

Elements of the 14th group are especially rich in allotropes. Graphite, diamond, nanotube, and β-tin are even used to label similar structures of other elements. The periodic trend in transformation of predominant forms of the 14th group elements – from graphitic structure carbon ($\mathbf{A}$) to diamond-like structure ($\mathbf{C}$) of silicon to β-tin structure of tin ($\mathbf{D}$ and $\mathbf{E}$), and finally to face-centered cubic (FCC) structure of lead ($\mathbf{F}$) – can be presented in the form of elongating a unit cell and/or shifting atoms’ positions as illustrated below.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-5-fig1.png

a) Determine the parameters of unit cells $\mathbf{A}$–$\mathbf{F}$. Here $\mathbf{B}$ is a hexagonal diamond structure.

None of the 14th group elements are present in nature as diatomic molecules. Yet, you can see the emission of photons from the excited $^3\Pi_\mathrm{g}$ state of $\ce{C2}$ formed in a flame of burning hydrocarbons. The ground state of the $\ce{C2}$ molecule ($^1\Sigma_\mathrm{g}$) differs from the ground state of other 14th group diatomics ($^3\Sigma_\mathrm{g}$).

b) Draw schematically and fill the MO diagrams of $\ce{C2}$ and $\ce{Si2}$.

c) Circle the correct options in the following text about $\ce{C2}$.

$\ce{C2}$ is a rare molecule without {σ, π, δ}-bonds, yet with two {σ, π, δ}-bonds. That is because the 2p orbital has {0, 1, 2} radial nodes, which gives the best orbital overlap ($S$) in forming π-bonds compared to $n$p orbitals, with $n > 2$. Also, as the energy of atomic orbitals ($\varepsilon_\mathrm{AO}$) is proportional to $n^{-2}$, the bonding MO energy ($\varepsilon_\mathrm{MO}$) is approximately $\varepsilon_\mathrm{AO}\cdot(1 + S)$, the π-bonds of C are much stronger than those of other 14th group elements. When excited to $^3\Pi_\mathrm{g}$ – a state with a bond order of {1, 2, 3} – $\ce{C2}$ relaxes by emitting a photon with $2.4\,\mathrm{eV}$ energy, which corresponds to {red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple} light. Eventually, $\ce{C2}$ produced in flame polymerizes into soot consisting of {diamond, fullerene, graphene, graphite, lonsdaleite, nanotube} entities.

For many solid structures, it is possible to choose a unit cell that contains two atoms, resembling a diatomic molecule. In the following figure, the orbitals are embedded into a unit cell of the diamond-type structure.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-5-fig2.png

d) Color in black-and-white the phase of the diatomic’s MO, so that the orbital energy of the resulting periodic orbitals increases from left to right.

In solids, combinations of $N$ orbitals give a so-called band, which corresponds to a range of allowed $N$ energy levels. Periodic repetition of the orbitals shown below corresponds to extreme energy levels. Similarly to how MOs are constructed in diatomic molecules, it is possible to use a diatomic’s MOs to form periodic orbitals for intermediate energy levels in bands. Namely, inverting half of the antibonding diatomics’ MOs in a $2\times2\times2$ unit cell gives the shown non-bonding periodic orbital. The inverted and non-inverted periodic orbitals set the upper and lower energy values for the corresponding antibonding s-band. The energy value between (or the average energy of) the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals is called the Fermi energy. Depending on whether the Fermi energy is within a band or in a band gap, an element can be a non-metal: an insulator (diamond) or a semiconductor (silicon); or a conductor: a semimetal (graphite) or a metal (lead). Electrical conductivity is the ability of electrons to move through a material, which depends on the proximity and density of energy levels above the Fermi energy.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-5-fig3.png

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/chemistry-olympiads-bank/main/images/bcho-2025-5-fig4.png

f) Estimate the band gap in diamond-type structure of C, Ge, and Pb solids, assuming that the highest occupied periodic orbital is due to the bonding p-orbital (from question d)) and the lowest unoccupied orbital is the shown non-bonding s-orbital. Assume that the energy of the bonding p-orbital is given by $\varepsilon_\mathrm{p}\cdot(1 + 2\cdot S)$ and $S \approx 4/9$. Take that orbital energies $\varepsilon_\mathrm{s}$ and $\varepsilon_\mathrm{p}$ equal to the negative value of ionization energies given in the table (in eV). Hint: This model predicts that Pb has a negative band gap, which means it is a metallic solid with zero band gap. The estimation yields reasonable agreement with known values, particularly for semiconducting silicon, whose band gap is closest to $1.1\,\mathrm{eV}$ for optimal performance of solar cells.

In terms of orbitals, a linear chain of carbon atoms – carbyne – has much in common with the FCC structure of lead, where atoms are also aligned. In both structures, pairs of p-orbitals combine in a similar way to form continuous π-bands with bonding and antibonding levels.

g) Show that combinations of bonding and antibonding MOs can give identical periodic orbitals, which means there is no band gap between bonding and antibonding bands. Hint: the drawing must have the same number of angular nodes, which (dis)appear upon inversion of MOs.

h) Circle the correct options in the following text about Pb.

In high-coordinated solids, the overlap ($S$) of a given orbital with neighboring orbitals is {lower, higher} than in low-coordinated ones. In the FCC structure, the overlap is {lower, higher}, leading to a {wider, narrower} p-band, in comparison to the diamond-type structure. Thus, the FCC structure is {stabilized, destabilized} by occupying the bonding p-orbitals. In the diamond-type structure, the antibonding {s, p, d}-band crosses the Fermi energy. Thus, the diamond-type structure is {stabilized, destabilized} by occupying the antibonding s-orbitals.

i) Generalize the explanation of why some group 14 elements are semiconductors with low coordination numbers, while others are conductors with higher coordination numbers.

• The crystal structure is favored when its geometry allows orbital overlap that maximizes bonding interactions and minimizes the filling of antibonding levels.
• The energy gap between s- and p-orbitals becomes smaller for heavier elements, which favours metallic bonding.
• The larger atomic radius of heavier elements prevents directional bonding, making the diamond structure geometrically unstable.
• Heavier elements have lower electronegativity, which favors metallic bonding.

Problem 4. Kinetics of formic acid electrooxidation (28 points, 12% of total score)

Electrooxidation of formic acid is a promising reaction for fuel cell applications. Depending on the catalyst materials, the electrooxidation proceeds by different mechanisms. Notably, the most common problem of CO poisoning is not observed on palladium catalysts. In this task we will explore the kinetics of formic acid electrooxidation on a palladium catalyst.

Before beginning the task, let us provide a brief background on kinetic analysis of electrochemical reactions on heterogenous catalysts. In general, we can distinguish between oxidation, reduction and non-electrochemical reactions:

$$\begin{array}{ll} A + {*} \xrightarrow{k_1} A{*} & \qquad \text{(non-electrochemical)} \\ A{*} \xrightarrow{k_2} A^+ + e^- + {*} & \qquad \text{(oxidation)} \\ A{*} + e^- \xrightarrow{k_3} A^- + {*} & \qquad \text{(reduction),} \end{array}$$

where * denotes empty surface site of the catalyst, and $\mathrm{A}{*}$ denotes particle $\mathrm{A}$ adsorbed on surface site of the catalyst.

The rate equations for those elementary reactions accordingly are:

$$\begin{aligned} r_1 &= k_1[A](1-\theta_A)\,, \\ r_2 &= k_2\theta_A e^{\alpha f E}\,, \\ r_3 &= k_3\theta_A e^{-(1-\alpha)fE}, \end{aligned}$$

where $1-\theta_A$ is the surface coverage of empty sites, $\theta_A$ is the surface coverage of $A{*}$ species, $\alpha$ is the reaction symmetry factor (usually considered to be 0.5), $f = \frac{F}{RT}$, and $E$ is the applied potential.

The current density dependence on applied potential $j(E)$ for an electrooxidation reaction can be expressed in terms of elementary rate equations as follows:

$$j(E) = F\sum r_{i,\mathrm{ox}} - F\sum r_{i,\mathrm{red}},$$

where $r_i$ are rates of oxidation and reduction steps.

The steps for the proposed mechanism for formic acid oxidation on palladium catalyst are as follows:

$$\begin{array}{ll} HCOOH + \mathbf{2}{*} \xrightarrow{k_1} HCOO{*} + H{*} & \qquad (1) \\ H{*} \xrightarrow{k_2} H^+ + e^- + {*} & \qquad (2) \\ HCOO{*} \xrightarrow{k_3} CO_2 + H^+ + e^- + {*} & \qquad (3) \\ HCOO{*} \xrightarrow{k_4} CO_2 + H{*} & \qquad (4) \\ H_2O + {*} \underset{k_{-5}}{\overset{k_5}{\rightleftharpoons}} OH{*} + H^+ + e^- & \qquad (5) \end{array}$$

1. Write the reaction rate equations for each of the elementary steps. (5 points)

2. Assuming steady state for all adsorbed species, obtain equations relating the rate equations. (3 points)

3. Write the expression for current density dependence on potential $j(E)$ in terms of reaction rate constants and surface coverages of adsorbates. (2 points)

4. Obtain expression for $\theta_H$ in terms of $\theta_{HCOO}$. (3 points)

5. Obtain implicit equation of the variation of $\theta_{HCOO}$ with potential. (9 points)

(Hint: The implicit equation should have a form of $\alpha\theta_{HCOO} + \beta\theta_{HCOOH}^{\frac{1}{2}} + \gamma = 0$, where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are coefficients to be determined dependant on concentrations, reaction rate constants, applied potential etc.)

6. Briefly explain how obtained equations can be used to obtain plots relating surface coverage with applied potential. (2 points)

Problem 5. A Basket Case (25 points, 10% of total score)

Basketane is a hydrocarbon which – as can be inferred from its name – structurally resembles a basket. This “wannabe cubane” was originally synthesized by Masamune, Cuts and Hogben in 1965 from the another no less curious hydrocarbon, $\mathbf{G}$.

In turn, compound $\mathbf{G}$ was first prepared from pseudopelletierine by the German chemist Richard Wilstätter exactly 60 years earlier. However, his original 7-step synthetic route was too long and complicated – so much so that American chemists were unable to reproduce it and even suggested that Wilstätter had in fact obtained not $\mathbf{G}$, but its isomer $\mathbf{J}$, a hydrocarbon widely used in polymer production.

Nevertheless, Wilstätter dispelled doubts about the structure of $\mathbf{G}$ by converting it into $\mathbf{H}$, a hydrocarbon already known in the literature and not obtainable from $\mathbf{J}$ in this way.

The synthesis of $\mathbf{G}$ remained highly challenging until 1948, when another German chemist, Walter Reppe, reported that compound $\mathbf{G}$ can be readily obtained from the common industrial gas $\mathbf{I}$ using a nickel(II) catalyst.

A slightly modified version of Wilstätter’s synthetic protocol is provided below.
